modules.title: Federal Incorporation (CBCA)
modules.short_description: Complete guide to incorporating a business under the Canada Business Corporations Act — from name search to post-incorporation compliance.
modules.long_description: Learn every step of the federal incorporation process. We cover NUANS name searches, preparing Articles of Incorporation, selecting directors, setting up share structures, filing with Corporations Canada, and all post-incorporation requirements including minute book setup, CRA registration, and ongoing annual maintenance obligations.

content.text:
What is a Federal Corporation?

A federal corporation is a legal business entity incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA). It is recognized across all provinces and territories and can carry on business anywhere in Canada under its corporate name.

Unlike provincial corporations, federal corporations have the right to use their corporate name nationwide and are subject to a single, national regulatory framework administered by Corporations Canada.

Key Characteristics

  • Separate legal entity distinct from its shareholders
  • Limited liability for shareholders
  • Perpetual existence — continues regardless of shareholder changes
  • Ability to own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued
  • Nationwide name protection under the CBCA
  • 25% Canadian resident director requirement

rows.right: Must be kept at registered office

key_concepts.definition: Canada Business Corporations Act — the federal statute that governs federally incorporated companies in Canada.
A corporation is legally distinct from its owners. It can own assets, incur debts, and be sued in its own name.
Shareholders are generally not personally liable for the corporation's debts beyond their investment.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Which Act governs federal corporations in Canada?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA) is the federal statute governing federally incorporated companies.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: What percentage of directors must be Canadian residents for a CBCA corporation?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: At least 25% of the directors of a CBCA corporation must be resident Canadians.

faq.q: Can a federal corporation operate in any province?
faq.a: Yes. A federal corporation has the right to carry on business in all provinces and territories. However, it must register extra-provincially in each province where it has a physical presence or employees.

faq.q: How is a federal corporation different from a provincial one?
faq.a: Federal corporations have nationwide name protection and a single regulator (Corporations Canada). Provincial corporations are governed by provincial law and must register extra-provincially to operate in other provinces.

faq.q: Can one person be the sole director, officer, and shareholder?
faq.a: Yes. A single individual can serve as the sole director, officer (President/Secretary), and 100% shareholder of a CBCA corporation — provided they meet the 25% Canadian residency requirement.

chapters.title: NUANS Name Search & Corporate Name Rules

content.text:
NUANS Name Search

Before incorporating, you must either choose a distinctive corporate name or use a numbered designation. If choosing a name, a NUANS search report is required.

NUANS (Newly Updated Automated Name Search) compares your proposed name against existing corporate names, trademarks, and business names across Canada to ensure it is not confusingly similar to an existing name.

Name Requirements Under the CBCA

  • Must be distinctive — not merely descriptive of the business
  • Must include a legal element: Ltd., Inc., Corp., Limited, Incorporated, Corporation
  • Cannot be confusingly similar to an existing corporate name or trademark
  • Cannot suggest government or Crown affiliation
  • Cannot include restricted words without approval (e.g., Bank, Insurance, Trust, University)

key_concepts.definition: Newly Updated Automated Name Search — a database search comparing proposed corporate names against existing names and trademarks.
A corporate name must be unique enough to distinguish the corporation from others. Descriptive names like 'Consulting Inc.' are generally rejected.
The mandatory suffix indicating incorporation: Limited (Ltd.), Incorporated (Inc.), Corporation (Corp.), or French equivalents (Ltée, Inc.).

knowledge_checkpoints.question: How long is a NUANS search report valid?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: A NUANS search report is valid for 90 days from the date of issuance.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Which is NOT required in a corporate name?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The owner's surname is not required. The name must be distinctive, include a legal element, and not be confusing with existing names.

faq.q: Do I need a NUANS search for a numbered company?
faq.a: No. Numbered companies (e.g., '12345678 Canada Inc.') do not require a NUANS search. The number is assigned automatically by Corporations Canada.

faq.q: What if my proposed name is rejected?
faq.a: Corporations Canada will notify you and give you an opportunity to submit a new name or amend the application. Having 2–3 backup options in your NUANS report helps avoid delays.

content.text:
Articles of Incorporation

The Articles of Incorporation is the foundational constitutional document of the corporation. It sets out the corporation's name, share structure, director provisions, and restrictions (if any). Preparing accurate and complete articles is the most important step in the incorporation process.

Required Elements

  • Corporate Name — Proposed name (with NUANS report) or numbered designation
  • Registered Office Address — Must be a physical address in the province of registration
  • Share Structure — Classes of shares, maximum number per class, rights and restrictions
  • Director Provisions — Minimum and maximum number of directors, residency requirements
  • Restrictions on Business — Any limits on the corporation's activities (if applicable)
  • Other Provisions — Any additional clauses required by the incorporators

key_concepts.definition: The maximum number of shares the corporation is authorized to issue, set out in the Articles. There is no statutory maximum under the CBCA.
The official address where corporate records must be kept. Must be in the province specified in the Articles.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Which of the following is NOT required in Articles of Incorporation?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The business number (BN) is assigned by the CRA after incorporation — it is not included in Articles of Incorporation.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Where must the registered office be located?
options: In the province specified in the Articles
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The registered office must be in the province specified in the Articles of Incorporation.

faq.q: Can I have multiple classes of shares?
faq.a: Yes. You can create multiple share classes (e.g., Class A voting common shares, Class B non-voting preferred shares) with different rights, privileges, restrictions, and conditions attached to each class.

faq.q: What is the minimum number of directors?
faq.a: A CBCA corporation must have at least one director. If the corporation is a distributing corporation (public), it must have at least three directors, at least two of whom are not officers or employees.

content.text:
After Incorporation: Critical Next Steps

Receiving the Certificate of Incorporation is just the beginning. A series of organizational steps must be completed promptly to ensure the corporation is properly constituted and compliant.

Immediate Post-Incorporation Tasks

  1. Organizational Meeting — Hold the first meeting of directors (or shareholders) to adopt bylaws, elect officers, issue shares, and approve corporate records
  2. Minute Book Setup — Create the corporate minute book containing bylaws, resolutions, share registers, director/officer registers, and transfer registers
  3. Share Issuance — Issue shares to the founding shareholders and record them in the securities register
  4. CRA Registration — Register for a Business Number (BN), GST/HST (if applicable), payroll deductions, and corporate income tax
  5. Provincial Registrations — Register for provincial taxes (PST/QST), workers' compensation, and any provincial licensing requirements

options: A 9-digit CRA identifier for tax accounts
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The Business Number is a 9-digit identifier assigned by the CRA for corporate tax, GST/HST, payroll, and other program accounts.

faq.q: Do I need a corporate seal?
faq.a: A corporate seal is not legally required under the CBCA, but many corporations choose to have one for traditional document execution. It is no longer mandatory.

faq.q: When must I register for GST/HST?
faq.a: You must register for GST/HST if your corporation's worldwide taxable supplies exceed $30,000 in any single calendar quarter or over four consecutive quarters. Voluntary registration is also available.

content.text:
Ongoing Compliance for Federal Corporations

Incorporation is not a one-time event. Federal corporations must comply with ongoing filing, record-keeping, and governance requirements under the CBCA. Failure to comply can result in administrative dissolution.

Annual Requirements

  • Annual Return — File within 60 days of the corporation's anniversary date. Includes director and registered office information.
  • Annual Meetings — Hold annual meetings of shareholders (AGM) within 15 months of the previous meeting. Directors must present financial statements.
  • Financial Statements — Prepare annual financial statements. Public corporations must file audited statements; private corporations must prepare them but filing is not always required.
  • Director/Officer Updates — Notify Corporations Canada of any changes to directors, officers, or registered office address within 15 days.
  • Minute Book Maintenance — Keep corporate records up to date: minutes of all meetings, resolutions, share transfers, and register changes.

events.title: Year-End Preparation
events.description: Prepare for next cycle, review corporate health

key_concepts.definition: A mandatory filing with Corporations Canada confirming the corporation's current directors and registered office address. Due within 60 days of the anniversary date.
Corporations Canada may dissolve a corporation that fails to file annual returns. The corporation can be revived, but the process involves additional fees and filings.
Annual General Meeting — a yearly meeting of shareholders required by the CBCA. Directors present financial statements, shareholders elect directors, and auditors are appointed (if applicable).

knowledge_checkpoints.question: When must the annual return be filed?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The annual return must be filed within 60 days of the corporation's anniversary date (the date of incorporation).

knowledge_checkpoints.question: What happens if a corporation fails to file annual returns?
options: The corporation may be administratively dissolved
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: Corporations Canada may administratively dissolve a corporation that fails to file annual returns. The corporation can be revived, but this adds cost and complexity.

faq.q: Can I file the annual return online?
faq.a: Yes. Corporations Canada offers online filing through their Online Filing Centre. Most returns can be completed in under 10 minutes.

faq.q: What is the penalty for late filing?
faq.a: There is no immediate financial penalty, but the corporation risks administrative dissolution if returns remain unfiled. Revival costs typically range from $200–$400.

chapters.title: What is a Corporate Minute Book?

content.text:
What is a Corporate Minute Book?

The corporate minute book is the official record of a corporation's legal and governance documents. It serves as the central repository for all corporate records and is the first thing reviewed during due diligence, financing, or a CRA audit.

Under the CBCA and provincial statutes, every corporation is legally required to maintain certain records at its registered office. The minute book is how these records are organized and preserved.

Why Minute Books Matter

  • Legal Compliance — Required by corporate statutes across all Canadian jurisdictions
  • Due Diligence — Buyers, lenders, and investors review minute books before transactions
  • CRA Audits — Minute books demonstrate corporate governance and support tax positions
  • Director Protection — Proper records protect directors from personal liability claims
  • Corporate Memory — Maintains a complete history of all corporate decisions and changes

key_concepts.definition: The bound or digital collection of a corporation's foundational documents, registers, minutes, resolutions, and share records.
Mandatory records required by corporate law: register of directors, register of officers, register of shareholders, and securities register.
The investigation process conducted by buyers, lenders, or investors to verify a corporation's legal standing, governance, and compliance history.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Are minute books legally required for Canadian corporations?
options: Yes — under the CBCA and provincial statutes
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: All Canadian corporations — federal and provincial — are legally required to maintain corporate records. The minute book is the standard way to organize these records.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Who typically reviews minute books during due diligence?
options: No one — minute books are private
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: During any transaction — financing, sale, investment — the counterparty's legal counsel will review the minute book to verify governance and identify gaps.

faq.q: Can a minute book be digital?
faq.a: Yes. Digital minute books are legally valid in Canada. Mortacc provides a complete digital minute book system with all required registers and documents.

faq.q: How far back should minute book records go?
faq.a: Records should go back to incorporation. Permanent records (articles, bylaws) must be kept indefinitely. Accounting records must be kept for 6 years from the end of the tax year.

content.text:
Required Documents in a Minute Book

A complete corporate minute book contains several categories of documents. Understanding what is required — and what should be included for best practice — helps ensure your corporation is audit-ready.

Statutory Registers (Mandatory)

  • Register of Directors — Names, addresses, dates of appointment/resignation, and residency status of all directors
  • Register of Officers — Names, positions, and dates of appointment/resignation
  • Register of Shareholders — Names, addresses, number and class of shares held, dates of issuance/transfer
  • Securities Register — Details of each share certificate issued, including certificate numbers, dates, and to whom issued

Additional Essential Documents

  • Certificate of Incorporation
  • Articles of Incorporation (and any amendments)
  • Bylaws (and any amendments)
  • Minutes of all shareholder and director meetings
  • Resolutions (signed written resolutions in lieu of meetings)
  • Share certificates (issued and cancelled)
  • Annual returns and filing confirmations

knowledge_checkpoints.question: Which register tracks who owns shares and when they were acquired?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The Register of Shareholders records share ownership — including names, addresses, share classes, numbers, and dates of issuance or transfer.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: What is a written resolution?
options: A resolution signed by all directors/shareholders in lieu of a meeting
A draft document that doesn't need signing
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: A written resolution is signed by all directors (or shareholders) and is legally equivalent to minutes of a formal meeting. It is a valid way to make corporate decisions without holding a physical meeting.

faq.q: Do I need a separate register for each class of shares?
faq.a: No. A single securities register can record all share classes, but each class should be clearly identified with its rights and restrictions noted.

faq.q: What if a share certificate is lost?
faq.a: The shareholder should sign a lost certificate affidavit and indemnity. The corporation can then issue a replacement certificate. This should be recorded in the minute book.

content.text:
Annual Minute Book Maintenance

Minute books must be updated annually. This is one of the most commonly neglected tasks in corporate governance — and one of the most important. An out-of-date minute book can cause serious problems during a transaction or audit.

Annual Update Checklist

  1. Annual Meeting Minutes — Document the AGM or pass written resolutions covering: approval of financial statements, election/re-election of directors, appointment of auditors (if applicable), and any other annual business
  2. Director Register Update — Confirm all directors are current; update terms, addresses, and residency status if changed
  3. Officer Register Update — Confirm current officers; record any appointments or resignations during the year
  4. Shareholder Register Review — Record any share transfers, issuances, or redemptions during the year
  5. Annual Return Filing — File with the appropriate registry and keep a copy in the minute book
  6. General Review — Check for missing documents, incomplete registers, or outdated information

content.text:
Digital Minute Books

Traditional minute books are physical binders. Modern corporate services practices are moving to digital minute books for efficiency, accessibility, and disaster recovery. Digital minute books are legally valid across all Canadian jurisdictions.

Advantages of Digital Minute Books

  • Accessibility — Access corporate records from anywhere, not just the physical registered office
  • Searchability — Find documents instantly rather than flipping through binders
  • Disaster Recovery — Cloud backup protects against fire, flood, or loss
  • Due Diligence Ready — Share a complete digital copy with legal counsel in minutes
  • Automatic Updates — Platform auto-generates annual documents and updates registers
  • Bilingual Support — Generate documents in English, French, or both simultaneously

content.text:
The Annual Corporate Maintenance Cycle

Every Canadian corporation — federal or provincial — must complete a set of annual compliance tasks. Understanding this cycle is fundamental to corporate services practice.

The Annual Cycle

Each year, corporations must: hold an annual general meeting (or pass resolutions in lieu), update statutory registers, file an annual return, prepare financial statements, and maintain their minute book. These tasks repeat annually for the entire life of the corporation.

For firms managing dozens or hundreds of entities, tracking deadlines across multiple jurisdictions becomes complex. A systematic approach — or automated platform — is essential to prevent missed deadlines.

content.text:
Deadlines by Jurisdiction

Each Canadian jurisdiction has its own annual filing deadlines and fee schedules. Understanding the differences is critical for multi-jurisdiction firms.

Federal (CBCA)

  • Annual Return: Within 60 days of anniversary date
  • Filing fee: $12 (online), $20 (paper)
  • No late fee, but risk of administrative dissolution

Ontario (OBCA)

  • Annual Return: Due with each filing (information update)
  • No separate annual return filing for private corporations
  • Changes must be filed within 15 days

British Columbia (BCA)

  • Annual Report: Within 2 months of anniversary date
  • Filing fee: ~$43.39 (online)
  • Late filing penalty applies

Québec (LSAQ)

  • Déclaration annuelle: Within 1 month of anniversary date
  • Filing fee: ~$89
  • Late fee: $108

key_concepts.definition: The registry may dissolve a corporation that fails to file. Revival is possible but involves additional cost and complexity.

knowledge_checkpoints.question: What is the annual return filing fee for a federal (CBCA) corporation?
knowledge_checkpoints.explanation: The online filing fee for a CBCA annual return is $12. Paper filing costs $20.

content.text:
Annual General Meeting Requirements

The AGM is a cornerstone of corporate governance. All Canadian corporations must hold an AGM or pass written resolutions in lieu. Understanding the requirements helps firms advise clients and maintain compliance.

Key Requirements

  • Must be held within 15 months of the previous AGM (18 months for the first)
  • Financial statements must be presented to shareholders
  • Directors are elected (or re-elected) at each AGM
  • Auditor appointed or audit waived (for private corporations)
  • Notice must be given to all shareholders entitled to vote
  • Written resolutions signed by all shareholders can replace a formal meeting

questions.question: What is the online filing fee for a federal annual return?
questions.explanation: The federal annual return filing fee is $12 when filed online through Corporations Canada.

questions.question: What does Mortacc auto-calculate for annual maintenance?
options: Deadlines based on incorporation date and jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Mortacc auto-calculates compliance deadlines per entity based on the incorporation date and jurisdiction-specific rules.
